meta.blurb: Edward Prendick is half dead from thirst when a ship picks him up, and its cargo is strange: caged animals and a silent servant. The last stop is an island where a doctor works in secret, and creatures chant strange rules.
meta.bible: Edward Prendick: a young English gentleman who studied natural science, the narrator, curious and kind but easily frightened. Montgomery: a former London medical student and Moreau's assistant, fond of drink, lonely, Prendick's only friend. Doctor Moreau: a brilliant, white-haired scientist, once driven from London for cruel experiments on animals; calm, cold and proud. M'ling: Montgomery's silent, faithful servant with a dark, strange face. Captain Davies: the drunken captain of the small ship Ipecacuanha. Lady Vain: the ship that sinks at the start. Ipecacuanha: the small ship that rescues Prendick. The Beast People: animals shaped by Moreau into human forms. The Sayer of the Law: the grey, bearded creature who leads the chant of the Law. The Law: rules for the Beast People; no walking on all fours, no lapping water, no eating flesh, no chasing other men. Dog Man: the gentlest creature, loyal to Prendick. Leopard Man: a creature who tastes blood and is hunted down. Hyena-swine: a savage mixture of hyena and pig who attacks Prendick. Ape Man: a chattering creature who talks nonsense. Puma: the big cat Moreau shapes into a woman. House of Pain: the Beast People's name for Moreau's laboratory. London. England. Pacific Ocean. The island. Voice and tone: eerie and thoughtful, a nightmare told calmly by an honest narrator; suffering and deaths are stated plainly and without gore; the book asks what separates a person from an animal.

B1B2: The ship Lady Vain has sunk after a terrible collision, and Edward Prendick has escaped in a small boat with two other men. They have almost no food or water, and there is no land in sight.
After days without enough water, the men begin to quarrel about the little food that is left. Two of them fight in the boat, fall into the sea and are lost, and Prendick is alone.
At last a small ship appears, and strong arms lift Prendick aboard. A young man named Montgomery gives him brandy and a bed, and Prendick sleeps for many hours.
The deck is crowded with cages holding rabbits, dogs and a big cat called a puma. Montgomery's servant, M'ling, has a dark, strange face that makes Prendick uneasy.
Prendick thanks Montgomery and asks where the ship is going, but the answers are short and strange. Montgomery says only that he was once a doctor in London and that the animals are for an island.
When the ship reaches the island, the drunken captain, Davies, refuses to carry Prendick any farther. Montgomery does not want a stranger on the island, but Davies will not listen to him.
Montgomery and M'ling row the boat toward a green island with a long white beach. A tall man with white hair is waiting on the shore, and he does not look pleased.
The tall man is Doctor Moreau, and Prendick is sure he has heard the name before. Slowly he remembers a scandal in London, when a doctor was driven out for hurting living animals in his experiments.
Moreau and Montgomery take the animals into a walled house and leave Prendick outside on the beach. Soon he hears the puma screaming inside, and he shivers with fear.
Montgomery lets Prendick into a small room, where he is given food and a bed. Yet the walls are thick, and every strange sound makes him sit up in fear.
Next day the screams grow louder, and now they sound like the cries of a woman or a man. Prendick is certain that Doctor Moreau is hurting a human being, and he cannot stay inside.
Prendick runs through the gate and into the thick green forest, with no plan except to get away. He pushes through the leaves until he reaches a stream and falls to his knees to drink.
Beside the stream, Prendick sees a hunched figure on hands and knees, drinking like an animal. When the creature raises its face, it is almost human, but its shape is not.
Prendick reaches a hidden camp of rough huts, where many strange creatures stare at him. One of them chants a Law, and the others join in, asking again and again, “Are we not men?”
Moreau and Montgomery arrive with guns and dogs, and the creatures fall to the ground in fear. Prendick is afraid of them, but Moreau promises to tell him the truth.
Moreau tells Prendick calmly that the creatures are not men but animals. With long, careful operations he has shaped them to walk upright, to speak and to follow rules.
Moreau describes the laboratory that the creatures call the House of Pain, where he works on each animal for days. He hopes that one day he will make a perfect, thinking person.
Moreau says that he does not enjoy hurting animals, but he believes that pain matters very little. Prendick, who has seen the creatures in their misery, cannot agree with him.
There is no ship, so Prendick must stay in the compound and wait. He and Montgomery slowly become friends, although Montgomery's loyalty to Moreau never changes.

Prendick learns the rules that Moreau has taught the Beast People, who must not walk on all fours, lap water or eat flesh. The creatures repeat them like a prayer, but Prendick doubts that fear will keep the rules alive.
One morning Prendick finds a dead rabbit in the forest. The Leopard Man has tasted blood and broken the Law, and a worried Moreau knows that others may follow him.
Moreau and Montgomery take their guns and their dogs to hunt the Leopard Man through the forest. Prendick goes with them because he is afraid to stay alone.
At last they find the Leopard Man in a dark thicket, and he fights back like a wild animal. Moreau shoots him, and the other Beast People watch from the trees and learn that the Law cannot be broken.
Moreau gathers the Beast People and says that the Law is for everyone, and that the Master sees everything. They bow their heads, but Prendick sees fear in their eyes and little understanding.
Moreau now works day and night on his greatest creation, a puma that he is shaping into a woman. Prendick can hear her screams from his room, and he is more disturbed than ever.
One afternoon the puma creature pulls loose from her ropes, breaks through the door and runs into the forest. Moreau, holding a gun, rushes out after her at once.
Moreau and Montgomery are quick, but Prendick soon loses them among the thick trees. He wanders alone for a long time, until at last he hears a cry and follows it.
Beside a small stream, Prendick finds Doctor Moreau lying still on the ground. Not far away lies the puma creature, and the long fight between them has ended in death for both.
Montgomery arrives, and together the two men carry Moreau's body back to the compound and lay it to rest. The Beast People watch from the forest, and they begin to ask where their Master has gone.
Montgomery, who has lost the only master he knew, begins to drink too much. Prendick pleads with him to stay calm, but he laughs and says that nothing matters now.
One evening Montgomery takes a barrel of drink out to the Beast People and tells them to be merry. Prendick follows, because he can see that a terrible mistake is about to be made.
Soon the Beast People forget the Law, and a wild fight begins around the fire. M'ling, the loyal servant, dies protecting Montgomery from the angry creatures.
Montgomery is killed in the fight, and in the confusion the boats are set on fire. Prendick sees that his only way off the island is burning on the beach.
The wooden house of the compound catches fire, and the flames light up the whole beach. Prendick takes what he can and runs for the forest, hoping that the darkness will hide him.
For days Prendick hides in the forest, hungry and afraid, eating fruit and drinking from streams. Every sound makes him jump, because he believes that the Beast People are looking for him.
One day the Dog Man finds Prendick and kneels before him as he once knelt before the Master. He is gentle and loyal, and he stays at Prendick's side as a servant and a friend.
Because he has no other choice, Prendick goes to live among the Beast People in their ravine. They treat him as a kind of master, and the days pass slowly.
Little by little the Beast People forget the Law and go back to their old, animal habits. They walk on all fours again, and their human faces seem to change a little each month.
One of the creatures, the Hyena-swine, is more savage than the rest, and he watches Prendick with hungry eyes. Prendick knows that he must always keep his gun close and sleep only lightly.
One evening the Hyena-swine leaps out at Prendick with a cry, and Prendick fires his gun. The creature falls, and the others, who saw it happen, run away in fear.
With the Hyena-swine gone, Prendick has a little peace, but he is more homesick than ever. Every morning he climbs a hill and searches the sea for a sail, and every evening he returns without hope.
The Ape Man still tries to talk and tells Prendick stories, but his words make less and less sense every day. Prendick feels pity for the creature, for there is nothing left of Moreau's plan.
One day a small boat drifts onto the beach with two men lying in it, and both are dead. Prendick does not know who they are, but he sees that the boat is still in good condition.
Prendick buries the dead men, fills the boat with fruit and water, and gets ready to leave. The Dog Man begs to come too, but Prendick cannot take him, and he sails alone.
Prendick drifts on the ocean for days, hungry and sunburnt, until a ship sees his small boat. The sailors lift him aboard, but when he tells them his story, nobody believes him.
Back in London, Prendick cannot feel safe among other people. Their faces remind him of the Beast People, and he fears that they, too, will turn back into animals.
Prendick finds that he cannot bear crowds, trains or lonely rooms at night. At last he leaves the city, hoping to find a quiet place in the country.
In the country Prendick finds a small house, books and a telescope, and he begins to study science again. He spends his evenings looking at the stars, and slowly his fear becomes smaller.
Prendick decides to write down everything that happened on the island, even though few people will believe it. He thinks often of Moreau, who tried to act like a god and who failed.

Prendick still sees something of the island in the faces of passing strangers, but his heart is calmer than it was. He believes that, somewhere above the world of men and beasts, there is something greater, and that thought brings him peace.
C1C2: In the year 1887, the ship Lady Vain struck a wreck in the Pacific Ocean and went down, and Edward Prendick, a young gentleman who had studied natural science, escaped in a small boat with two other men. The boat carried almost no food and only a little water, and for days the horizon showed nothing but empty sea. Prendick, who had expected to be rescued within hours, began to understand how small a boat is on the ocean.

As the days passed, thirst turned the men against one another, and a bitter quarrel broke out over the last of the food and water. Two of them fought in the narrow boat, fell into the sea together, and were lost beneath the waves. Prendick was left alone, half mad with thirst, drifting under a burning sky with nothing to do but wait.

At last a small sailing ship appeared out of the glare, and Prendick, too weak to cry out, was lifted aboard by strong hands. A young man named Montgomery gave him brandy and a bed, and for many hours he slept as though he were dead. He woke to find that he was safe, though the ship, he soon discovered, carried a very odd cargo.

The deck of the little ship was crowded with cages holding rabbits, dogs, llamas and a great tawny puma, which snarled at every passer-by. Montgomery's servant, M'ling, was a silent figure with a dark, curiously shaped face, and his eyes shone green when the lantern caught them. Prendick, grateful for his rescue, tried not to stare, but he felt a chill whenever the man came near.

Prendick thanked his rescuer and asked where the little ship was bound, but Montgomery gave short, evasive answers that only deepened the mystery. He admitted that he had once studied medicine in London, and that the animals were wanted on a small island in the Pacific where he lived and worked. When Prendick pressed him for more, he changed the subject, and a shadow seemed to fall across his friendly face.

When the island came into view, the ship's captain, a drunken, quarrelsome man named Davies, declared that Prendick must leave the vessel at once. Montgomery protested, for he plainly did not want a stranger on his island, but the captain would not listen to him or to anyone else. Prendick was put into a small boat, and the ship swung away, leaving him with the doctor, the servant and the animals.

Montgomery and M'ling bent to the oars, and the boat, heavy with animals, crept toward a green island that rose from the sea in a long line of low hills. On the white beach stood a tall, white-haired man, who watched the boat with a grave face and no sign of welcome. Prendick, soaked and exhausted, had no idea that he was about to meet one of the strangest men alive.

The tall man was Doctor Moreau, and as Prendick heard the name, a memory stirred in his mind. Years before, in London, a famous scientist of that name had been driven out of the country after a newspaper revealed that he had performed cruel experiments on living animals. Prendick wondered whether this quiet, white-haired man could be the same person, and whether his rescue had been a stroke of luck or of the worst misfortune.

Moreau and Montgomery carried the animals into a walled enclosure beside the sea and shut the gate, leaving Prendick alone on the beach. Before long, from somewhere inside, came the terrible cries of the puma, rising and falling like the voice of a person in pain. Prendick, who had suffered so much already, felt his skin creep with horror, and he shivered in the warm night air.

In the end, Montgomery came out, gave Prendick food and showed him a small room inside the compound, but the cries of the animals made rest impossible. Moreau, in his white coat, kept to his workroom and did not speak to the guest, and the whole house seemed to be hiding something. Prendick lay awake, listening to the sea and wondering what kind of place he had come to.

On the next day the cries came again, and now they sounded to Prendick less like an animal than like a person pleading to be spared. He remembered the old scandal and was seized by a wild fear that Moreau was practising his cruel science on human beings. He could bear it no longer, and snatching up his hat, he rushed from the room.

Prendick burst through the open door and ran across the beach, plunging into a forest of tall ferns and thick, tangled trees. He had no plan, no weapon and no knowledge of the island, but he hurried on until he came upon a small stream, where he stopped, panting, to rest. It was there, beside the cool water, that he first saw one of the strange inhabitants of the island.

A hunched, half-clothed figure was bending over the water, lapping at it on all fours like an animal, and when it lifted its face, Prendick saw something horribly wrong. The features were those of a man, yet the head was oddly shaped and the eyes had a strange glow. Terrified, Prendick turned and ran, while the creature rose and followed him step by step.

Soon the frightened Prendick came upon a hidden camp of rough huts, where several more of the strange creatures stood watching him with sly, wondering faces. One of them, a grey figure with a heavy beard, stepped forward and began to chant a strange Law, and the others joined in, asking again and again, “Are we not men?” Prendick, who had never felt so lost, realised at last that he had stumbled upon the dark secret of the island.

Moreau and Montgomery appeared among the trees with guns and dogs, and at the sight of Moreau, the strange creatures dropped to the ground in fear. Prendick, who still thought the doctor a monster, shrank away, but he was weak, hungry and unarmed, and in the end he allowed himself to be led back. Moreau promised that every question would be answered, and for the first time his voice sounded almost kind.

Sitting in his study with a lamp between them, Moreau explained, with the patience of a teacher, that the strange creatures were not men at all but animals. By means of long, careful operations, and by a patient training of their minds, he had shaped them to walk upright, to speak and to follow rules. It was, he said, the work of his life, and nothing in the world could persuade him to give it up.

Moreau described the laboratory that the creatures called the House of Pain, where each animal was worked upon for days and weeks before it was turned loose upon the island. His aim, he said, was to create a being that could reason, speak and rule over its own instincts, a perfect and thinking creature in a human shape. Prendick listened with a growing sense of dismay, for the plan was bold, but it was also cruel.

Moreau insisted that he took no pleasure in the pain of the animals, and that he was neither angry nor cruel but simply absorbed in his work. Pain, he argued, was a small thing, a signal that mattered less to a thinking being than to a beast. Prendick, who had heard the puma's cries and seen the creatures in the forest, knew that he could never agree.

There was no ship to carry him away, and Prendick had to wait on the island with these two men and their secrets. In the following weeks, he and Montgomery became friends of a kind, talking in the evenings about London, books and the strange creatures in the forest. Prendick was grateful for the friendship, but he noticed that Montgomery's loyalty to Moreau did not change.

Prendick came to know the rules that Moreau had taught to the Beast People, which forbade them to walk on all fours, to lap water, to eat flesh or to chase other men. Every few days, the creatures gathered in a ring and recited the Law, and Moreau's fear of the whip and of the House of Pain kept them obedient. Prendick, watching the strange ceremony, wondered how long fear alone could keep the beasts from remembering what they had been.

One morning, Prendick found a dead rabbit lying in the forest, and beside it the signs that something had fed upon it. The Leopard Man, one of Moreau's creatures, had tasted blood and broken the most important rule of all, and when Moreau heard the news, his face grew dark with worry. If one of the beasts could break the Law and escape punishment, he said, then all of them might begin to do so.

Moreau ordered that the Leopard Man must be found at once, and with Montgomery and the dogs, he led a hunt through the forest. Prendick, who preferred to be with armed men than to wait alone in the compound, followed them. Slowly the party moved through the ferns, following the tracks of a creature that had once been taught to be a man.

At last the hunters cornered the Leopard Man in a dark thicket, where he turned on them with the savage fury of a wild beast. Moreau, cool and steady, shot him dead, and the other creatures, who had crept up to watch from the trees, saw what happened to those who broke the Law. Prendick turned away, sickened, and walked home in silence, unable to forget what he had seen.

Moreau summoned the Beast People and warned them in a loud, solemn voice that the Law was for everyone, and that the Master could see every secret deed. They bowed their heads and moaned together, repeating the words they had been taught, but Prendick saw only fear in their eyes and little real understanding. The danger, he felt, had not passed at all, but had merely sunk out of sight below the surface.

Moreau now devoted all his time to his boldest experiment, the shaping of the puma into a creature with a woman's form. For days the sound of her cries, rising and falling, came through the walls of the laboratory, and Prendick, listening, could hardly eat or sleep. He told himself that he would soon leave the island, though he knew that no ship was likely to come.

One afternoon, with a great effort, the half-finished creature tore loose from her bonds, burst through the door of the laboratory and fled into the forest. Moreau, who had been working over her, was horrified to see his greatest hope escape, and he snatched up his gun and ran out after her. Montgomery, shouting and half dressed, hurried after him, and Prendick, uncertain what else to do, followed.

Moreau and Montgomery were fast, but Prendick, weak from his long ordeal, soon lost sight of them among the thick trees. For a long time he wandered alone, calling and listening, while the afternoon light grew thin. At length, from a long way ahead, there came a cry, and he hurried towards it with his heart beating hard.

In a hollow beside a small stream, Prendick came upon a sight that he would never forget, for Doctor Moreau lay dead upon the ground. A short distance away lay the puma creature, who had fought for her freedom and lost her life in the struggle. The great experimenter, who had made so many creatures suffer, had been brought down by the last and most unhappy of them.

Montgomery soon arrived, and together the two men carried the body of Moreau back to the compound and laid it to rest. From the edge of the forest, the Beast People watched in silence, and Prendick saw that they did not yet understand that their Master was gone. When they did, he knew that nothing on the island would ever be the same.

Montgomery, who had lost the only master he had ever known, began to drink heavily, and soon he was seldom sober. Prendick pleaded with him to keep a clear head, for the Beast People were restless, but the doctor only laughed and said that nothing mattered any more. Every day, he grew a little more reckless, and Prendick grew a little more afraid.

One evening, Montgomery lost all caution and carried a barrel of strong drink out into the forest, calling to the Beast People to come and be merry with him. They gathered around the fire, laughing and howling, and drank until they forgot every rule they had been taught. Prendick, watching from a distance, saw that a great and terrible mistake was being made that night.

As the night went on, the Beast People forgot the Law, and the laughter turned to quarrelling, and the quarrel turned to a wild fight. M'ling, who had served Montgomery faithfully, threw himself in front of his master and fell. Prendick, rooted to the spot, saw that the whole island was about to turn against the humans who ruled it.

Montgomery was struck down in the fight and did not rise again, and in the confusion, the boats on the beach were set alight. Prendick, who had hoped to use one of them to escape, watched his only way off the island burn to ashes. The darkness filled with howls, and he understood that he was now entirely alone among the creatures.

Before long, the walled house caught fire, and the flames lit the whole beach with a dull, angry glare. Prendick snatched up a few things and ran for the forest, hoping that the darkness would hide him from the creatures who were now free of every master. He did not look back, for he could not bear the sight of the burning house.

For several days, Prendick hid in the forest like a hunted animal, living on fruit and water and starting at every sound. He believed that the Beast People were searching for him, and he knew that if they found him, he could not hope for mercy. It was a lonely, dreadful time, and he began to wonder whether he would ever see another human face.

One day, the Dog Man, who had always been gentler than the other creatures, found Prendick in his hiding place and knelt before him as he had once knelt before the Master. He had the loyalty of a faithful hound, and he stayed at Prendick's side, guarding him and bringing him what food he could. In his strange, patient devotion, Prendick found the first comfort that he had known for weeks.

Because there was nothing else to be done, Prendick went to live among the Beast People in their ravine, and they received him with a kind of puzzled respect. He had a gun, and they remembered that he had been the Master's guest, so they allowed him to be the strange man who shared their fire. Month after month, the days passed slowly, and he waited for a ship that did not come.

Little by little, the Beast People forgot the Law and returned to their animal habits, so that the days became a slow, sad lesson in how quickly civilisation fades. First one, then another dropped to all fours, and their speech grew thick and then died away into grunts and growls. Prendick watched the human shapes slip away from their faces, and he mourned for what Moreau had tried to build.

One of the creatures, a savage mixture of hyena and pig whom the others called the Hyena-swine, grew bolder with every passing week, and he watched Prendick with a hungry, calculating gaze. He whispered to the others that the stranger was weak, that the Master was dead, and that the Law was a thing of the past. Prendick kept his revolver within reach, and he slept only in snatches, lightly, like a hunted animal.

One evening, in the half-light, the Hyena-swine leapt from the bushes with a roar, and Prendick, who had been waiting for the attack, fired his revolver at him. The creature fell and lay still, and the others, who had watched from a distance, turned and fled into the trees. After that day, no one on the island dared to challenge the man with the gun.

With the Hyena-swine gone, a little peace returned to the ravine, though it was a cold and lonely peace. Every morning, Prendick climbed the hill above the beach to search the sea for a sail, and every evening, he came down again, a little more discouraged than the day before. The only living thing that understood his sorrow was the Dog Man, who sat beside him and said nothing.

The Ape Man, who had once been the cleverest of the creatures, still tried to talk, and he chattered at Prendick for hours in a language that made less and less sense. Prendick listened out of pity, remembering how proudly the creature had once recited the Law. There was nothing now but noise, and nothing remained of Moreau's great and dreadful plan.

One morning, a small boat drifted onto the beach with two men lying in the bottom of it, and both were dead. Prendick never discovered where they had come from, or what storm or hunger had killed them, but he saw at once that the boat was still sound. For the first time in months, he felt something that he had almost forgotten, and it was hope.

Prendick buried the dead men, filled the boat with fruit and water, and prepared to push off from the shore. The Dog Man, who had been his faithful friend for so long, begged with his eyes to be taken along, but Prendick knew that a creature of the island could never live among men. With a heavy heart, he said goodbye and let the current carry him away.

For days, Prendick drifted across the empty ocean, hungry and sunburnt, until at last a passing ship saw his little boat and took him aboard. The sailors were kind to him, but when he told them where he had been and what he had seen, they looked at him in disbelief. Soon he learned to say nothing, for he saw that to be thought mad would make his life impossible.

Back in England, among the busy streets and comfortable houses, Prendick found that he could not shake off the island. In every crowd, he seemed to see a face with the shadow of an animal behind it, and every conversation sounded to him like the jabbering of the Ape Man. He feared that the people around him would slowly slip back into their old, wild habits.

His fear grew, until he could no longer bear to ride on a crowded train, to sit in a church or to walk down a busy street. Although he knew that his terror was foolish, he could not make himself believe it, and friends and relations saw that something was wrong. At last he left the city for good and sought out a quiet corner of the country.

In the country, Prendick found a small, quiet house, and he filled it with books on chemistry and astronomy, subjects that had little to do with living creatures. On clear nights, he climbed a hill and looked up at the stars, which shone calmly and endlessly above the troubles of men. Slowly, as the seasons turned, the memory of the island grew a little fainter.

In the end, Prendick wrote down everything that had happened to him, knowing well that few people would believe the tale. He thought often of Moreau, a brilliant and fearless man who had tried to take the part of a creator, and who had made only suffering. The lesson that he drew from it was not a clever one, but he never forgot it, for it concerned the limits of what a person may do to another living creature.

Even now, Prendick sometimes sees the island in the faces of passing strangers, and he knows that the memory will never leave him entirely. Yet when he stands alone on the hill and looks at the stars, a great calm settles over him, and the fears of the world seem small and far away. In that quiet, he finds the hope that the long, cruel story had threatened to take from him, and it is with that hope that his own tale ends.
